full_judgment:
3. The plaintiffs stated, inter alia, that the suit land is situated at locality Roy Hussain known as Amberkhana, Sylhet town and the same belonged to Karamatullah and others. The said owners used to hold and possess the suit land through their tenants Amu Singha and Garuba Singha. Karamatullah and others sold the suit land to Md. Irfan Ali Chowdhury by registered kabala dated 28.02.1927 and made over possession to him. Said Irfan Ali Chowdhury was the original plaintiff of the suit and died during pendency of the suit and was substituted by the present plaintiffs. The suit land comprises plot No.2 and western part of plot No.1 as per the said kabala. Irfan Ali Chowdhury used to hold and possess the suit land through said Amu Singha and Garuba Singha. Subsequently, Amu Singha took settlement of the suit land from him for one year by registered kabauliyat dated 27.07.1927 and used to live there till his death in 1342 B.S. 

 8. It is further stated that although the heirs of Amu Singha surrendered possession of the suit land to the original plaintiff in 1342 BS, it was wrongly referred to as 1362 B.S. in the plaint of Title Suit No.301 of 1966. Therefore, the plaintiff filed the instant suit for declaration of title and recovery of vacant khas possession upon removing structure, mesne profit and permanent injunction restraining the defendant opposite parties from changing the nature and feature of the suit land. 

 9. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement stating, inter alia, that the suit land belonged to Amu Singha in fate right who took settlement from the original plaintiff by executing kabuliyat dated Ashar 1344 B.S. While Amu Singha was living therein, he died leaving his son Krishna Singha, who died unmarried leaving his only nephew (sister's son) defendant No.2 as his only heir. Accordingly, defendant No.2 held and possessed the suit land. During settlement and survey operation the suit land was recorded in the name of Krishna Singha noting the name of the original plaintiff as landlord. The plaintiff in collusion with the Objection Officer changed the record-of—right in his name. Defendant No.2 then filed appeal under section 19(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which was allowed on contest on 09.09.1961. The further case of defendant No.1 is that defendant No.2 was possessing the suit land partly as homestead and partly as chara bari (abandoned homestead) and then he transferred part of the suit land as noted in schedule II of the written statement by kabala dated 07.08.1965 to defendant No.1 and delivered possession. Defendant No.1 has been possessing part of the suit land purchased by him as stated above by constructing but and planting trees. The plaintiff is cunning and he took defendant No.2 in his confidence with high hopes that he would buy the land at a high price. Defendant No.2 having decided to sell part of the suit land to defendant No.1 began to kill time and refused presentation of kabala for registration and defendant No.1 then presented the kabala dated 07.08.1965 for registration before the Sub-registrar. Defendant No.2 did not appear at the instance of the plaintiff. So defendant No.1 had to file appeal before the District Registrar and the kabala was registered on contest on 02.02.1966. The plaintiff and defendant No.2 are in collusion and under influence of the plaintiff, defendant No.2 is remaining silent. 

 14. Mr. Qumrul Hoque Siddique, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent No.8 made submission in support of the impugned judgement-and order of the High Court Division. He also submitted that neither the trial Court nor the appellate Court took into consideration the contents of Exhibit- `Ga'(sale deed in favour of defendant No.1-predecessor of the appellants) which shows that Gopendra Singha was in possession of the suit land on payment of rent to the original owner Irfan Ali Chowdhury. Subsequently, he claimed the property by inheritance from Krishna Singha, and thus the story of inheritance by Gopendra Singha from Krishna Singha is falsified. Hence, the High Court Division was correct in reversing the decision of the Courts below, even though their findings were concurrent. He further submitted that the wife of Amu Singha surrendered the land to the plaintiff. He further submitted that the Courts below failed to appreciate Exhibits 2 and 3 and did not consider the evidence of P.Ws 1 to 5, who unequivocally deposed that dispossession took place on Chaitra, 1373 BS after defendant No.2 executed the deed on 07.08.1965 in favour of defendant No.1 and wrongly held that the plaintiff failed to prove his dispossession. The learned Advocate also submitted that the Courts below failed to consider material facts on record showing that defendant No.2 was not a tenant under the original plaintiff nor was he the heir of Amu Singha, and hence no title passed to defendant No.1. He further submitted that the High Court Division correctly found and observed that defendant No. 2 illegally dispossessed the plaintiff in Chaitra, 1373 BS and defendant No.1 did not produce any rent receipt or any other papers to show that Krishna Singha was a tenant of the plaintiff. Moreover, Gopendra Singha did not come to support the claim of defendant No. 1. He lastly submitted that the original plaintiff was in possession of the suit land through tenants W.C. Keymer and his wife Rosemary by registered lease deed dated 1944. They handed back possession of the property to the original plaintiff after two years of the tenancy. 

 18. With regard to the possession by the plaintiff through tenant W.C. Keymer, the finding of the trial Court is that there was no witness to support the claim that Rosemary and her husband ever went into possession of the suit land. P.Ws 2 and 3 stated in their cross-examination that they did not know Rosemary. P.W.1, though she stated that Rosemary remained in possession of the suit land for two years and then handed back possession to Irfan Ali Chowdhury, the trial Court noted that there was no evidence to show that possession was handed back nor that Rosemary took possession of the suit land from Krishna Singha or Gopendra Singha. The trial Court concluded that Rosemary did not get possession of the suit land and that her letter of settlement was only a paper transaction. 

 21. We note that the High Court Division mentioned that the trial Court after hearing the parties, without considering the evidence on record, wrongly and illegally dismissed the suit. However, we note from the impugned judgement that the High Court Division did not specifically refer to any of the evidence and materials on record to show which evidence the Courts below did not consider. The deed, by which Irfan Ali Chowdhury got the suit property is indeed very old. However, subsequent events and documents relating to those later events tend to indicate that Irfan Ali Chowdhury was no longer in possession of the suit land. On the contrary the evidence of the witnesses shows that defendant No.2 and his predecessors-in-interest were all along in possession of the suit land. We note that Krishna Singha, the predecessor of defendant No.1 got his name recorded in the record of rights as tenant, which the original plaintiff got corrected. But thereafter, Gopendra Singha (defendant No. 2 who sold the suit property to defendant No.1) filed an appeal under section 19(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and got his name recorded in the record of rights. Khodeja Akhter Chowdhury who is the daughter of Irfan Ali Chowdhury deposing as P.W 1 could not controvert such claim. She admitted that her father's challenge against the record of rights was not fruitful. She also could not say whether her father took the matter further on appeal under section 53 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. We note that P.W 1 stated in her evidence that her father took possession of the suit land in 1342 BS (c.1935 AD), whereas PW4 stated that in 1950 Manipuri people lived on the suit land. Coincidentally, in Title Suit No.301 of 1965, Irfan Ali Chowdhury had claimed that possession of the suit land had been handed over to him in 1362 BS. (c.1955 AD). Moreover, we note that P.W1 stated in her deposition that 1362 BS was mistakenly written and that the correct date was 1342. This is clearly falsified by the evidence of P.W4.
